en: Thus have I heard: the Mahācattārīsakasutta, the 117th discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you noble right concentration together with its proximate cause and its requisites.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is noble right concentration with its supports and its requisites? That is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Now, bhikkhus, that one-pointedness of mind which is supported by these seven factors—”
This, monks, is called noble right concentration with its proximate cause and its equipment.
In this regard, monks, right view comes first.
And how, monks, does right view come first?
One understands wrong view as "wrong view" and right view as "right view"—this is one's right view.
And what, monks, is wrong view?
"There is no giving, there is no offering, there is no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and evil deeds."
‘There is no result of kamma; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; and there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge and make them known.’”
This, monks, is wrong view.
And what, monks, is right view?
Monks, I say that right view is twofold: [the mundane and the supramundane].
“Monks, there is right view that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions;
and there is, monks, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
And what, monks, is right view that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions?”
‘There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of good and evil deeds;
there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings of spontaneous birth;

there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world by their own super-knowledge and make them known to others.’
‘Having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, they make it known’— this, monks,
is right view that is still subject to taints, partaking of merit, and ripening in the acquisitions.
And what, monks, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path?

"Monks, that which is the wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, and the right view as a path-factor of one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path, and who is developing the noble path—this, monks, is called right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
He exerts himself for the abandoning of wrong view and for the attainment of right view; this is his right effort."
Thus, being mindful, one abandons wrong view and, having entered upon right view, dwells therein; this is one’s right mindfulness.
In this way, these three qualities run alongside and revolve around right view, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Among them, monks, right view is the forerunner.
And how, monks, does right view come first?
One understands wrong intention as "wrong intention" and understands right intention as "right intention"—this is one's right view.
And what, monks, is wrong intention?
Thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty—
this, monks, is wrong intention.
And what, monks, is right intention?
“Bhikkhus, I say that right intention is twofold:
there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is tainted, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions;
and there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.”
And what, monks, is right intention that is still subject to taints, partaking of merit, and ripening in the acquisitions?
Right intention of renunciation, right intention of non-ill will, and right intention of non-cruelty:
this, monks, is right intention that is still subject to taints, partaking of merit, and ripening in the acquisitions.
And what, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path?

It is, monks, the thought, applied thought, intention, absorption, sustained application, the directing of the mind, and the verbal formation of one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path,
and who is developing the noble path— this, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
Thus, he strives for the abandoning of wrong intention and for the attainment of right intention; this is his right effort.
Mindfully, he abandons wrong intention and, having attained right intention, he dwells therein; this is his right mindfulness.
Thus these three qualities run alongside and revolve around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
In this regard, monks, right view comes first.
And how, monks, does right view come first?
One understands wrong speech as "wrong speech" and understands right speech as "right speech"; that is one's right view.
And what, monks, is wrong speech? False speech,
malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—
this, monks, is wrong speech.
And what, monks, is right speech?
Monks, I say that right speech is twofold:

there is, monks, right speech that is subject to taints, partaking of merit, and ripening in the acquisitions; [and there is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path].
"There is, monks, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
And what, monks, is right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions?
It is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter."
“Monks, this right speech is subject to taints, partakes of merit, and results in the acquisitions.
And what, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path?

It is, monks, the refraining, abstaining, desisting from, and avoiding of the four types of verbal misconduct by one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path, and who is developing the noble path.”
This, monks, is right speech: noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
He makes an effort for the abandoning of wrong speech and for the undertaking of right speech; this is his right effort.
Mindfully he abandons wrong speech, and mindfully he dwells having undertaken right speech; this is his right mindfulness.
Thus these three qualities run and circle around right speech; that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
In this regard, monks, right view is the forerunner.
And how, monks, is right view the forerunner?
One understands wrong action as "wrong action" and right action as "right action"; this is one's right view.
And what, monks, is wrong action?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
This, monks, is wrong action.
And what, monks, is right action?
Right action, monks, I declare to be twofold: [the worldly and the supramundane].
“Monks, there is right action that is tainted, partaking of merit, and resulting in the acquisitions;
there is, monks, right action that is noble, untainted, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
And what, monks, is right action that is tainted, partaking of merit, and resulting in the acquisitions?”
Abstaining from the destruction of life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct— this, monks,
is right action that is subject to taints, partakes of merit, and results in the acquisitions.
And what, monks, is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path?

“Monks, whatever abstaining, desisting, refraining, and abstinence from the three types of bodily misconduct there is on the part of one with noble mind, with taintless mind, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path—this, monks, is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
He exerts himself for the abandoning of wrong action and for the undertaking of right action; this is his right effort.”
Thus, being mindful, one abandons wrong action and, having entered upon right action, dwells therein; this constitutes his right mindfulness.
In this way, these three factors run alongside and revolve around right action, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Among these, monks, right view is the forerunner.
And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first?
One understands wrong livelihood as "wrong livelihood" and understands right livelihood as "right livelihood"; that is one's right view.
And what, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood?
Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain—
this, monks, is wrong livelihood.
And what, monks, is right livelihood?
“Monks, I declare that right livelihood is twofold:
there is, monks, right livelihood that is tainted, partaking of merit, and ripening in the acquisitions;
and there is, monks, right livelihood that is noble, untainted, supramundane, and a factor of the path.”
"And what, monks, is right livelihood that is with taints, partaking of merit, and resulting in acquisition?
Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood— this, monks,
is right livelihood that is with taints, partaking of merit, and resulting in acquisition."
And what, monks, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path?
It is, monks, the refraining from, abstaining from, desisting from, and avoiding wrong livelihood in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path,
and who is developing the noble path— this, monks, is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
Thus he makes an effort for the abandoning of wrong livelihood and for the undertaking of right livelihood; this is his right effort.
Mindfully he abandons wrong livelihood, and mindfully, having undertaken right livelihood, he dwells; this is his right mindfulness.
Thus these three qualities run alongside and revolve around right livelihood, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
In that regard, monks, right view is the forerunner.
And how, monks, is right view the forerunner?
For one with right view, monks, right intention arises; for one with right intention, right speech arises.
For one of right speech, right action arises; for one of right action, right livelihood arises; for one of right livelihood, right effort arises;
for one of right effort, right mindfulness arises; for one of right mindfulness, right concentration arises;
for one of right concentration, right knowledge arises; for one of right knowledge, right liberation arises.
Thus, monks, one in training is endowed with eight factors, and an arahant is endowed with ten factors.
Therein, too, through right knowledge, many evil unwholesome states are removed and reach fulfillment through development.
And therein, monks, right view is the forerunner.
And how, monks, does right view become the forerunner?
For one with right view, monks, wrong view is worn away;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are also worn away in him.
With right view as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
For one with right intention, monks, wrong intention is worn away...
For one with right speech, monks, wrong speech is worn away.
“Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is worn away… monks,
for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away… monks,
for one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away.”
“Monks, for one with right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away;
monks, for one with right concentration, wrong concentration is worn away;
monks, for one with right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away.”
“Monks, for one who is rightly liberated, wrong liberation is worn away.
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are also worn away.
And conditioned by right liberation, many wholesome states reach fulfillment through development.”
"Thus, monks, there are twenty factors on the side of the wholesome and twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome.
This exposition of the Dhamma, the Great Forty, has been set forth, and it cannot be overturned by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
For whatever ascetic or brahmin, monks, [should refute] this Great Forty exposition of the Dhamma..."
If one were to think that [right view] should be censured and rejected, then ten legitimate grounds for censure would apply to him in this very life: "If you,
sir, censure right view, then those ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong view are worthy of honor by you and are to be praised by you."
If you, sir, censure right intention, then those ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong intentions are worthy of honor by you and are to be praised by you.
If you, sir, censure right speech...
[and so on] ...if you, sir, censure right action...
If you, sir, censure right livelihood … if you,
sir, censure right effort … if you,
sir, censure right mindfulness …
If you, sir, disparage right concentration… if you,
sir, disparage right knowledge… if you,
sir, disparage right liberation, then those ascetics and brahmins who possess wrong liberation are worthy of honor by you, they are praiseworthy by you.
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetic or brahmin might think that this discourse on the Dhamma in forty sections should be censured or rejected,
ten legitimate grounds for censure come upon him in this very life.

Even those Okkalā Vassa-bhajjā, bhikkhus, who were proponents of non-causality, proponents of non-action, and proponents of nihilism— even they did not think that this discourse on the Dhamma in forty sections should be censured or rejected.”
"And for what reason?
Out of fear of blame, reproach, and censure.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Great Discourse on the Forty, the seventh, is finished.
